Writing systems. A structured set of symbols and rules for encoding human language into visible marks, allowing thought and speech to be preserved and transmitted across time and space.

All writing systems solve the problem of mapping discrete language units onto a visual medium, but they differ radically in what units they represent. Alphabetic systems like Latin letters are phonemic, assigning one symbol per consonant or vowel sound. They require learning twenty to thirty symbols and are theoretically more efficient for transcribing new vocabulary. Logographic systems like Chinese characters or Egyptian hieroglyphics assign meanings to individual symbols and require learning hundreds or thousands of distinct signs, but they allow readers to grasp meaning regardless of pronunciation. Syllabic systems like Japanese kana assign one symbol per syllable, offering a middle ground between phonetic precision and a manageable symbol inventory, and they enabled democratic literacy in Heian Japan. Abjads, like Arabic and Hebrew, represent only consonants, omitting vowels, so readers must rely on linguistic knowledge to disambiguate meaning from consonant sequences alone.

The invention of writing, roughly thirty-two hundred BCE in Mesopotamia and Egypt, was not immediate or monolithic. Scripts evolved from accounting tokens and pictures into systematic notation over centuries, driven by practical need for taxation, ritual, and commerce.

Different scripts carry cultural prestige and power. Prestige scripts exclude non-learners and concentrate authority, while phonetic scripts democratize literacy. The adoption of kana in Heian Japan gave women literary voice for the first time. Writing systems are not neutral transcriptions of speech. They shape how writers think about language itself, privilege certain linguistic structures over others, and embed the values of their creators into every marked page.
